title: F1 teams await decision on Bahrain, Saudi Arabia races after Middle East war
content:
SHANGHAI — Formula 1 teams continue to await a decision on the running of the upcoming races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, with a call anticipated by early next week.

F1 is currently scheduled to hold its fourth and fifth rounds of the 2026 season in Bahrain (Apr. 12) and Saudi Arabia (Apr. 19), but the running of both events has been thrown into doubt by the unfolding conflict in the Middle East.

F1 issued a statement shortly after the first missile strikes in the region saying it was closely monitoring the ongoing conflict, which has already prompted the FIA, F1’s governing body, to cancel its World Endurance Championship sports car event in Qatar that was scheduled for later this month.

No decision has yet been communicated to F1’s 11 teams or wider paddock personnel, but it is anticipated to arrive by early next week at the latest following this weekend’s Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

This would come before the cut-off for more freight being sent to the Bahrain International Circuit, which is just 20 miles from a United States army base that was targeted by Iranian strikes earlier this month.

As recently as Monday, the official X account for the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix was still promoting ticket sales for the race.

But members of F1’s leadership, including CEO and president Stefano Domenicali, remain in close contact with authorities in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, as well as the promoters of the races about the viability of any event going ahead.

Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time F1 world champion who drives for Ferrari, expressed faith in the right call being made on the running of the races.

“I know that Stefano will do what’s right for all of us and the sport,” Hamilton told reporters in Shanghai on Thursday. “That’s the great thing with having a good leader like him.”

Asked on Thursday when the teams needed to know if the races would be taking place, Haas F1 chief Ayao Komatsu replied: “Last week.”

“Honestly the sooner (we know), the better,” added Komatsu. “I’m sure obviously F1 is dealing with things that I’m not aware of. I don’t know. But obviously as a team, the sooner we know, the better. We’ve got to know this week for sure. I’m sure we will.”

Following the staging of preseason testing in Bahrain last month, teams have left some freight at the circuit which they are currently unable to access. The UK Foreign Office has advised against “all but essential” travel to Bahrain, with the same advice in place for parts of Saudi Arabia.

Komatsu said that the equipment in Bahrain was “all set up,” and that “even if we want to move it, we need to send someone to pack those up, which is impossible.”

“Whatever is in Bahrain isn’t going anywhere,” said Komatsu. “It’s a big problem. Honestly the sooner we know, the better.”

Should both grands prix be cancelled, F1 is not anticipated to seek replacement events due to the logistical challenge of finding another track at short notice and the burden this would place on teams.

That would provisionally leave a five-week gap between the Japanese Grand Prix on Mar. 29 and the Miami Grand Prix on May 3, as well as reducing the calendar to 22 races for 2026.

Mike Krack, the chief trackside officer of Aston Martin, suggested that teams had to remain open in their plans for any eventualities, but said there was confidence in F1 and the FIA to “make the right decision” over the races.

“I think F1 teams are very flexible organisations that are quite reactive,” said Krack. “So we will deal with whatever is being decided, and I am sure that the correct decision will be made.”
